subject: technology
essential_question: How do we build something substantial and prove, at each step, that it works?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Algorithms and Programming
project_brief: Build the capstone system to a testable milestone with verified requirements, automated tests, and accessibility evidence. This is the grade 12 culminating project for "Capstone Design, Build, and Test" (ma-g12-technology-u05, unit 5), built around problem validation and stakeholders, requirements and success metrics, architecture and build increments, verification and test evidence, and accessibility and privacy verification. Build the capstone system to a testable milestone with verified requirements, automated tests, and accessibility evidence. As you build this, trace through your logic by hand for at least one representative input or scenario before you run or finalize it, so you can compare your prediction with the actual result.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: problem validation and stakeholders, requirements and success metrics, architecture and build increments, verification and test evidence, accessibility and privacy verification, and iteration from feedback.
Meet the performance task as written: Build the capstone system to a testable milestone with verified requirements, automated tests, and accessibility evidence.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Build the capstone system to a testable milestone with verified requirements, automated tests, and accessibility evidence. As you build this, trace through your logic by hand for at least one representative input or scenario before you run or finalize it, so you can compare your prediction with the actual result.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to problem validation and stakeholders or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.
The algorithm or program handles at least one edge case (empty input, zero, an unexpected choice) without crashing or giving a wrong answer silently.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering problem validation and stakeholders in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to requirements and success metrics, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
